content.overview: BNS s. 56 — Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment. BNS restatement of IPC 116. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 116. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 56 is the rule on “Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment”. The section provides that whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 56 exists so that “Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
56. Whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made under this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence; or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both

learningObjectives: Understand inchoate abetment of ordinary imprisonment offences under BNS s. 56.
Analyze the fractional sentencing rule: up to one-fourth of the longest term.
Identify the aggravated penalty for public servants: up to one-half.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 56 provides that whoever abets an offence punishable with imprisonment shall, if that offence be not committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence for a term which may extend to one-fourth part of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both; and if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, whose duty it is to prevent the commission of such offence, the abettor shall be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for that offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the longest term provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for that offence, or with both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Unsuccessful abetment of non-capital offences is punished fractionally at one-fourth of the maximum statutory term, doubled to one-half if a public servant tasked with crime prevention is involved.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 56 (corresponding to IPC s. 116).
Offence category: Offences punishable with imprisonment (other than capital/life under s. 55).
Condition: The offence abetted is NOT committed in consequence.
General Rule: Imprisonment up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both.
Aggravated Public Servant Rule: If abettor or person abetted is a public servant duty-bound to prevent the crime, imprisonment up to one-half of longest term, or fine, or both.
essentialIngredients: The accused abetted an offence punishable with imprisonment.
The offence was not committed in consequence of the abetment.
General penalty: Up to 1/4th of the maximum term or fine or both.
Aggravated penalty: Up to 1/2 of the maximum term if a public servant with a duty to prevent is the abettor or person abetted.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 56 governs all unconsummated abetment of ordinary offences such as theft, extortion, assault, or cheating. The law uses a mathematical proportion: the abettor receives up to one-fourth of the maximum sentence prescribed for the crime he attempted to cause. However, if the abettor attempts to corrupt a police officer (a public servant duty-bound to prevent crime) by offering a bribe to permit smuggling, or if the police officer himself instigates a crime, the penalty is doubled to one-half because official duty has been subverted.
examples: Teaching example (Failed theft instigation): A instigates B to steal goods from a store (theft max penalty 3 years). B refuses. The theft is not committed. Under s. 56, A is liable to imprisonment up to one-fourth of 3 years (9 months) or fine.

Teaching example (Bribing police officer): A offers a police sub-inspector a bribe to allow illicit contraband through a checkpoint. The officer refuses and arrests A. As the officer is a public servant duty-bound to prevent the crime, A is liable under s. 56 to imprisonment up to one-half of the maximum term.
distinctions: Section 55 vs Section 56: Section 55 applies to capital/life offences (fixed 7/14 years); Section 56 applies to all other imprisonment offences (one-fourth / one-half fraction).
General abettor vs Public servant involved: Public servant involvement doubles the exposure from one-fourth to one-half.
problemApplication: Issue: What is the liability of an individual who urged an accomplice to commit house-trespass (max penalty 1 year), where the accomplice declined to proceed?
Rule: Under BNS s. 56, unsuccessful abetment of an imprisonment offence is punished with up to one-fourth of the maximum term.
Application: The offence is punishable with 1 year; one-fourth is 3 months. The abettor is a private citizen.
Conclusion: The individual is liable to imprisonment up to 3 months, or fine, or both.

shortAnswer: State BNS s. 56 rule on failed abetment of imprisonment offences.
State the general fraction: up to 1/4th of the longest term.
State the public servant aggravated fraction: up to 1/2 of the longest term.
